teaser: One stick. Two chalk marks. A smaller shadow at noon.
title: Shadows at Noon
question: Why is a shadow shorter at noon?
idea: Around noon, the sun is near its highest point for the day. A standing stick casts a shorter shadow than when the sun is lower.

curiosity.intro: One stick. Two chalk marks. Why did the shadow change?
curiosity.carryForward: Follow the sunlight, compare the lengths, and keep a small clue.

questions.question: How can we save a shadow’s length?
questions.notice: Little puts a chalk mark at the long shadow’s tip.
questions.say: A shadow forms where an object blocks sunlight. Mark its tip, then measure from the standing stick to the mark. Use the same measuring stick and unit to compare both lengths.
questions.try: With Big, measure from the stick’s base to its shadow tip. Keep your eyes on the ground; never look at the sun.

questions.question: Why is the noon shadow so short?
questions.notice: The same standing stick now has a short, crisp shadow.
questions.say: Around noon, the sun is near its highest point in the sky for the day. Light reaches the ground from higher above, so the stick’s shadow stays closer to its base. A lower morning or afternoon sun makes a longer shadow.
questions.try: Compare the short shadow with the earlier chalk mark.

questions.question: Which way does a shadow point?
questions.notice: One side of the stick is bright. The shadow is on the other side.
questions.say: The bright side faces the sun. The stick blocks some sunlight, leaving a shadow that points away from the light. Follow the shadow along the ground.
questions.try: Point from the bright side, past the stick, toward the shadow.

questions.question: What clue can a short shadow give us?
questions.notice: Little keeps a long line and a short line in the notebook.
questions.say: A short noon shadow is a clue that the sun is high. Compare the same standing stick in the same place, using the same unit. Chalk marks and notes help us remember what changed. Measuring can lead to another question.
questions.try: Ask one new question about tomorrow’s shadow.

outline.arc: Little saves a long morning shadow, returns to find a short noon shadow, follows the direction of the light, compares two lengths, and keeps a clue in a notebook.

beatIntents.intent: Establish the same vertical wooden stick in a pale garden path, a long morning shadow, Big and Little, chalk, and linen notebook; begin with a question.
Little saves the long shadow tip with one chalk mark; use a closer ground-level composition with the same unmoved stick.
Return at noon to the same stick; show a short crisp shadow and the earlier chalk mark farther away.
Focus on the mechanism: light on one side of the vertical stick, short shadow on the opposite side; Big and Little attend to the ground.
Compare morning and noon chalk marks with the same wooden measuring stick; notebook records the evidence.
Close with two simple notebook lines and the short shadow beside the pair; invite a new question.

beats.title: A morning question
beats.passage: Little Wonderer found a long shape beside a standing stick. It was a shadow: a place where the stick blocked sunlight, the light from the sun. “Will it stay this long?” Little asked. Big set a linen notebook beside the garden path. They had a question to keep.

beats.title: Save the tip
beats.passage: Little took a piece of chalk, a soft stick for making marks. “First mark the tip,” said Big. Little drew a small line where the shadow ended. To measure is to find how long something is. They used a measuring stick from the wooden stick’s base to the chalk.
beats.prompt: Why did Little mark the tip?

beats.title: A smaller patch
beats.passage: At noon, the middle of the day, they came back. The wooden stick had stayed in place, but its shadow had changed. “It is short and crisp!” said Little. Around noon, the sun is near its highest point for the day. The morning shadow had reached much farther.
beats.prompt: What changed between morning and noon?

beats.title: Follow the light
beats.passage: “Which way does it point?” asked Big. Little studied the ground. Sunlight reached one side of the stick. The shadow stretched away on the other side. The bright side faced the sun; the shadow pointed away from the light. Little traced its edge along the ground with one finger.
beats.prompt: Which way does a shadow point?

beats.title: Compare the marks
beats.passage: Little marked the new tip with chalk. They used the same measuring stick to check both lengths. They began at the same standing stick and used the same unit each time. The noon length was shorter. “The stick stayed the same,” Little said. “The sun’s height changed.”
beats.prompt: Why use the same unit each time?

beats.title: A clue to keep
beats.passage: In the notebook, Little drew a long line for morning and a short line for noon. Later, when the sun was lower, the shadow would grow longer again. A short noon shadow was a clue to a high sun. “What will we notice tomorrow?” Little asked.

math.title: Count equal groups in the sunshine
math.intro: Each group has the same number. Add the equal groups or rows to find the total.

tasks.prompt: Little draws 2 rows of chalk marks on the path, with 3 marks in each row. How many chalk marks are there?
tasks.hint: Add one row at a time: 3 + 3.
tasks.worked: 3 + 3 = 6. Two rows of 3 make 6 chalk marks.
tasks.label: TASK 1

tasks.prompt: Big sets out 3 groups of measuring pebbles, with 4 pebbles in each group. How many pebbles are there altogether?
tasks.worked: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. Three groups of 4 make 12 measuring pebbles.
tasks.label: TASK 2

tasks.prompt: Little lays sticks in 4 rows in the sunny yard, with 2 sticks in each row. How many sticks are there?
tasks.hint: Add the sticks in each row: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2.
tasks.label: TASK 3

tasks.prompt: A shadow notebook has 2 rows of boxes, with 5 boxes in each row. How many boxes are there?
tasks.worked: 5 + 5 = 10. Two rows of 5 make 10 notebook boxes.
tasks.label: TASK 4

tasks.prompt: Little draws 5 groups of shadow-tip dots in the notebook, with 3 dots in each group. How many dots are there?
tasks.worked: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 15. Five groups of 3 make 15 shadow-tip dots.
tasks.label: TASK 5

tasks.prompt: Big draws 5 rows of chalk circles beside the shadow, with 5 circles in each row. How many circles are there?
tasks.hint: Add one row at a time: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5.
tasks.worked: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 25. Five rows of 5 make 25 chalk circles.
tasks.label: TASK 6

math.extension: Choose one task. Draw its equal groups or rows and tell how the addition matches your drawing.

parentGuidance: Age 8, Grade 3 reading, and Grade 2 math. This story uses a sunny yard at middle latitudes. Solar noon is when the sun reaches its highest point that day; it need not be 12:00 by the clock. For the same vertical stick on level ground, that gives the shortest daytime shadow. The sun’s height varies with place and season; in Illinois it is never directly overhead. Clear sunlight gives a distinct edge; clouds can soften it. The diorama isolates sun height and light direction, with equal chalk spaces for comparison, not a clock or local forecast. The math counts equal groups and rows of garden and notebook objects. For an optional outdoor try, an adult helps place a stable blunt stick beside a path. Enjoy watching the shadow on the ground; never look at the sun.

authoring.learningRule: Leo is age 8, Grade 3 for reading; math is Grade 2. New Curiosity packs declare mathTemplate and require exactly six tasks for that template. Every number (operands, terms, intermediates, answers) is an integer from 0 to 100. Each task asks one clear question tied to the day's story and includes an equation matching the validated numbers, a hint, numeric answer, and short worked explanation containing the answer (mixed-review retains its shipped calculation rule). Replace scaffold notebook objects with the day's story objects. Explain precise vocabulary in context; welcome speech and dictation. Template groups-and-arrays: Six equal-group/array tasks, both skills present. Store rows and columns, each 2–5. Equation is rows copies of columns joined by + and ending in =, never multiplication. Hint shows a repeated sum.

questions.prompt: In this sunny yard, what happens to the same stick’s shadow around noon?
choices: It becomes longer as the sun rises
It is shorter when the sun is high
questions.answer: Around noon, the sun is near its highest point for the day, so the same standing stick has a shorter shadow.

questions.prompt: What happens to the shadow when the sun is lower?
choices: The shadow always stays the same
questions.answer: A lower sun makes a longer shadow from the same standing stick.

questions.prompt: Which way does a shadow point?
questions.answer: A shadow points away from the light. The bright side of the stick faces the sun.

questions.prompt: How can Little compare morning and noon shadows?
choices: Move the stick to a new place each time
Mark both tips and measure from the same stick with the same unit
Guess from the color of the chalk
questions.answer: Keep the stick standing in the same place. Mark each tip and measure from the stick with the same unit, then compare the lengths.
